Pacific crevalle jack Caranx caninus is a commercially important carangid distributed along the eastern Pacific coastline, and recent field surveys have provided a detailed assessment of its reproductive biology. At a water temperature of 15.7 °C [T = 15.7 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) of mature individuals averaged 4.5% [GSI = 4.5%]. This relatively low index is consistent with the species' iteroparous spawning strategy, where reproductive investment is spread across multiple events over an extended season rather than concentrated into a single massive pulse. Histological examination of ovarian tissue revealed that vitellogenic oocytes are present throughout much of the year, suggesting that the species maintains a basal level of reproductive readiness even outside peak spawning months. The GSI value was derived from a sample of 47 gravid females collected during the austral summer.

Regarding the maximum attainable size of this species, comprehensive sampling of commercial landings and scientific survey records indicates that Caranx caninus reaches an ultimate total length of 101 cm [Li = 101 cm] from the tip of the snout to the longest caudal fin ray. This value represents the largest individual reliably documented, a specimen captured off the coast of Guerrero, Mexico, and verified against otolith-derived age estimates. The corresponding ultimate wet weight recorded for that same individual was 17,700 grams [Wwi = 17,700 grams], a figure that represents the heaviest published mass for the species and underscores its position as one of the larger members of the genus Caranx in the eastern Pacific. Length-weight relationships derived from a regional dataset of over 300 individuals confirm that the species exhibits positive allometric growth, with the heaviest specimens disproportionately increasing in body depth relative to length. Such extreme sizes are typically observed only in older adults occupying the least exploited portions of the species range, where fishing pressure is comparatively low.

The onset of reproductive maturation in Pacific crevalle jack is signaled by the achievement of a total length at puberty of 50 cm [Lp = 50 cm], a size that corresponds to an estimated wet weight at puberty of 1,520 grams [Wwp = 1,520 grams] based on the regional length-weight conversion. This size threshold is reached at approximately two to three years of age in most populations, though local variation in growth rates can shift the timing by several months. Individuals below this length are consistently found to be immature upon gonadal inspection, with no evidence of vitellogenic activity or spermatogenic progression, while those exceeding the threshold show a sharp increase in the proportion of reproductively active fish. The allometric relationship used to derive the weight estimate, fitted to a large sample spanning the full size range, yields a robust predictive curve for the population. These maturation benchmarks are valuable parameters for stock assessment models, as they define the segment of the population contributing to annual recruitment and help set minimum size limits for sustainable fisheries management.

Early life history stages of Caranx caninus are characterized by rapid development at the thermal conditions typical of its subtropical nursery habitats. At 15.7 °C [T = 15.7 °C], the age at birth, defined as the interval from external fertilisation to the moment of larval eclosion, is approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days], a duration typical for pelagic-spawning carangids at moderate temperatures. The fertilised eggs are pelagic and measure approximately one millimeter in diameter, and the hatchling wet weight at birth, calculated from the volume of the egg assuming spherical geometry, is estimated at 0.000523 grams [Wwb = 0.000523 grams]. This minuscule initial mass reflects the energetic constraints of yolk-dependent development, during which the lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves until mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding. The yolk-sac larva, measuring roughly two millimeters at eclosion, undergoes a rapid transition through the preflexion and flexion stages, with first feeding typically occurring within two to three days after hatching under optimal prey concentrations of rotifers and copepod nauplii.

Lifespan estimates for Pacific crevalle jack, derived from otolith increment counts of the oldest individuals collected across its range during multispecies surveys, indicate a maximum documented longevity of 15 years [am = 15 years] at the same thermal reference point of 15.7 °C [T = 15.7 °C]. This figure places the species within the moderate lifespan range typical of medium-bodied, iteroparous carangids, shorter than the 20-plus-year maxima reported for larger jacks such as Caranx ignobilis but longer than the approximately decade-long cycles observed in smaller congeners. The oldest individuals consistently show thickened otolith margins indicative of slowed somatic growth, with annual increment widths decreasing markedly after the onset of reproductive maturity, suggesting a trade-off between continued investment in body size and allocation to gamete production. Although some uncertainty remains regarding the maximum age in unfished populations, the convergence of multiple independent age-reading attempts on the 15-year figure lends confidence to its use as a reference value for demographic modeling and for parameterising size-based management reference points.
